query: For high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could improve hardness and strength without sacrificing useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to produce the improvement, a measurable outcome relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with clear observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of titanium to high-entropy alloys can improve hardness and strength without sacrificing useful mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: High titanium content may lead to brittle phases
generation.uncertainty: Optimal titanium content for balanced strength and ductility is unknown

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of titanium does not improve hardness and strength, or if it leads to a significant decrease in ductility, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: From the images in Fig. 3, the nano-twins in the EBSD scans become very clear by overlaying the scan on an image quality, IQ, map of the same data set, which permits the measurement of the typical misorientation angle of 60° for twinning (Fig. 3e). We conclude from these results that between room and cryogenic temperatures where the strength, ductility and toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi are all simultaneously enhanced, nano-twinning contributes an important additional deformation mode that helps alleviate the deleterious effects of high strength that would normally be expected to result in lower toughness.

One of the most investigated HEA systems is AlCoCrCuFeNi and the copper-free derivate AlCoCrFeNi [,]. Distinct improvement of mechanical properties can be achieved by alloying with titanium. Due to its large atomic radius, the addition of titanium causes solid–solution strengthening and hence increased strength and hardness. Additionally, the formation of brittle phases was observed for a high content of titanium [,,]. The wear resistance of the alloy system AlCoCrFeNiTi has been investigated under various conditions revealing an increased wear resistance, also in comparison with the steels EN 1.3505 and EN 1.3343 [,]. Although improved high-temperature properties of AlCoCrFeNiTi are expected, the wear behaviour has not yet been investigated at increased temperature.
